overview: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its last meeting before next Tuesday's midterm elections, though two officials voted for a hike with inflation at 3.7%. Abroad, a high-speed train crashed into a stopped train south of Madrid, killing at least 68 people; Israel's election left Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc short of a majority; and defeated Brazilian candidate Flávio Bolsonaro flew to Miami while under investigation at home. In Washington, a grand jury declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her Jan. 6 testimony, and President Trump said he is ending Biden-era limits on methane from oil and gas drilling. stories.headline: Grand jury declines to indict former Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson over Jan. 6 testimony
stories.summary: A federal grand jury in Washington declined to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide whose 2022 testimony described President Trump's conduct on Jan. 6, 2021, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the AP, CNN and Fox News. Prosecutors had sought charges alleging she lied to Congress. Reports said it was unclear whether the Justice Department would try again.
stories.why_it_matters: Grand juries made up of ordinary citizens must agree before most federal charges go forward, and several outlets described this as the latest in a series of failed attempts to charge people the president sees as adversaries. The case also bears on whether witnesses who testify to Congress can later be prosecuted over their accounts; outlets across the spectrum reported it.
stories.background: Hutchinson was a top aide to Mark Meadows, President Trump's last White House chief of staff. In June 2022 she testified publicly to the House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, describing what she saw and heard of Trump's actions that day; Trump and some of his allies disputed parts of her account. In early October, Punchbowl News reported that the Justice Department was seeking to indict her on allegations that she lied to lawmakers. The effort is one of several the department has pursued against people Trump has publicly criticized, some of which have stalled in court or before grand juries.

facts.text: A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., declined to indict Hutchinson over her testimony about the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, according to people familiar with the matter.
Prosecutors had sought to charge her over statements she made to the House Jan. 6 select committee, alleging that she lied to Congress.
Punchbowl News reported in early October that the department was seeking an indictment and that prosecutors from its Civil Rights Division had presented evidence to a grand jury.

NBC News reported that the failed indictment is one of many for federal prosecutors during Trump's second term; the AP and The Wall Street Journal called it the latest setback in the department's efforts to charge people Trump views as adversaries.
Hutchinson's lawyers did not respond to requests for comment, CNN reported.

stories.headline: Trump says he is ending Biden-era limits on methane from oil and gas drilling
stories.summary: At a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, President Trump said his administration is 'terminating' a Biden-era rule meant to cut methane emissions from oil and gas operations. The Environmental Protection Agency is proposing a rewrite that the administration says will save $45 billion. Environmental groups say the change would exempt many of the highest-polluting wells.
stories.why_it_matters: Methane leaks from wells and pipelines add to climate change and waste natural gas; the administration argues the rules drive up energy costs, while critics say loosening them means more pollution. A proposed rule normally goes through public comment before it can take effect.
stories.background: Methane, the main ingredient in natural gas, traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in its first couple of decades in the atmosphere, and oil and gas operations are a major source. In 2024 the Biden administration's EPA finalized rules requiring companies to find and fix leaks, phase out routine flaring and respond to large leaks flagged by outside monitors through a 'super emitter' program. Small producers and many oil-state Republicans opposed the rules as costly. Under Administrator Lee Zeldin, the EPA made narrower changes in April 2026 and previewed a broader rewrite in early October.

facts.text: Trump said at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday that his administration is 'terminating' Biden-era methane regulations for oil and gas companies.
The Washington Free Beacon reported before the rally that Trump would announce an EPA proposal rolling back the Biden-era limits.
Trump cited $45 billion in savings; the Free Beacon described it as savings for Americans in energy costs.
In early October, Zeldin said the EPA was days away from proposing the changes, and the agency said the rollback would save $45 billion in regulatory costs, Source NM reported.

According to Source NM, the proposal would eliminate the super emitter program, which lets outside parties report large leaks for operators to fix, and would offer options for regulating low-producing 'marginal' wells.
Small fossil-fuel producers have opposed the rules, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The Environmental Defense Fund said the changes would create loopholes for low-producing, high-polluting well sites, which it says supply less than 5% of U.S. oil and gas but produce more than half of the industry's methane emissions.
In April 2026, the EPA finalized two narrower changes to the Biden-era methane rule.

stories.headline: Trump rallies for Paxton in Texas as Talarico holds rival event in Lubbock
stories.summary: A week before the Nov. 3 midterms, President Trump held two rallies in Texas on Tuesday to help Republican Ken Paxton in a close U.S. Senate race against Democrat James Talarico. Paxton and Talarico held dueling events in Lubbock on either side of a city park, where Talarico vowed to 'take back Texas.' Democrats call the race their best chance in a generation to win a Senate seat in the state.
stories.why_it_matters: Texas is one of a handful of races that could decide which party controls the Senate, which confirms judges and cabinet members and shapes which bills become law. Most of the coverage came from left-leaning outlets; Fox News focused on a speaker at a Talarico rally who called for abolishing ICE.
stories.background: Ken Paxton, Texas's Republican attorney general, won his party's Senate nomination by defeating Sen. John Cornyn in a May runoff. James Talarico, a Democratic state representative and former teacher, is trying to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988. Polls have shown a close contest, and Trump has traveled to the state repeatedly in the campaign's final weeks. Lubbock, in West Texas, is a heavily Republican city.

Before the trip, Fox 4 in Dallas-Fort Worth reported that recent polling showed Talarico with a one-point lead.

stories.headline: Dolores Huerta, farmworker organizer and United Farm Workers co-founder, dies at 96
stories.summary: Dolores Huerta, the labor and civil rights organizer who co-founded what became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez, died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on Instagram. She coined the rallying cry 'Sí, se puede' and kept working on immigration and voting issues late in life. Earlier this year she said publicly that Chávez had raped her decades ago.
stories.why_it_matters: Huerta helped win wage, safety and bargaining protections for farmworkers, the mostly Latino laborers who pick much of the country's fruit and vegetables, and her slogan became a widely used political rallying cry. Outlets across the spectrum covered her death.
stories.background: Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930 and grew up in Stockton, California, where she worked as a teacher before turning to organizing. In 1962 she and Chávez founded the National Farm Workers Association, which led strikes and a national grape boycott and later became the United Farm Workers. She negotiated contracts with growers and lobbied for laws protecting farmworkers, and President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. In March 2026, after a New York Times investigation reported that Chávez had sexually abused women and minors, Huerta said he had pressured her into sex in her 20s and later raped her.

facts.text: Huerta died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on social media.
She co-founded the United Farm Workers with César Chávez.

NBC News wrote that her work improved the lives of the country's mostly Latino farmworkers and changed the course of the labor movement.

In March, Huerta told ABC News that Chávez pressured her into sex when she was in her 20s and later raped her, and that she had two children as a result whom she arranged to be raised by other families.
Her account followed a New York Times investigation that reported Chávez had groomed and sexually abused women and minors.

stories.headline: Alexander brothers, once top luxury real estate brokers, each sentenced to 30 years for sex trafficking
stories.summary: A federal judge in Manhattan on Tuesday sentenced Tal and Oren Alexander, once prominent luxury real estate brokers, and their brother Alon to 30 years in prison each for sex trafficking. Eleven women spoke at the hearing about being drugged and raped. The brothers, convicted in March, said the case is 'far from over.'
stories.why_it_matters: The sentences close the trial phase of one of the most prominent sex-trafficking prosecutions in years, a case in which prosecutors said wealth and social status were used to lure women. The brothers have said they will appeal.
stories.background: Tal and Oren Alexander were well-known brokers of high-end homes in Miami and New York, and their brother Alon worked in private security. They were arrested in December 2024 and charged with sex trafficking after dozens of women accused them of drugging and assaulting them at parties and on trips over more than a decade. A federal jury in Manhattan convicted all three in March 2026 after a five-week trial in which 11 women testified. Prosecutors asked for life sentences; the brothers maintain their innocence.

stories.headline: Judge rules Trump's top prosecutor in Los Angeles is not lawfully serving
stories.summary: A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli, who runs the U.S. attorney's office in Los Angeles under the title of first assistant, is unlawfully serving as the office's top prosecutor. Essayli, a Trump ally and former Republican state lawmaker who has not been confirmed by the Senate, said the Supreme Court will ultimately decide the question.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling adds to court decisions questioning how the administration has kept prosecutors in charge without Senate confirmation, an issue defense lawyers have used to challenge criminal cases. Essayli's office handles federal cases for the Los Angeles area, the country's most populous federal court district.
stories.background: U.S. attorneys are normally nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and federal law limits how long interim or acting officials can serve. Essayli was named interim U.S. attorney for the Central District of California in 2025; when his 120-day term ran out, the Justice Department kept him in charge as first assistant. In October 2025, Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled that he could not serve as acting U.S. attorney but let him keep supervising cases as first assistant. Defense lawyers renewed their challenge after the Ninth Circuit appeals court ruled against a similar arrangement for Nevada's top federal prosecutor, Sigal Chattah, which the Justice Department has taken to the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: U.S. and Cuban officials trade shouts at the U.N. during embargo debate
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuban officials got into a shouting match on the floor of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday during debate on Cuba's yearly resolution calling for an end to the U.S. economic embargo. Waltz had accused Cuba's government of corruption and of profiting from its citizens' forced labor; he later posted video of Cuban officials standing and speaking while he was at the podium.
stories.why_it_matters: The resolution is non-binding, and only Congress can fully lift the embargo, which has limited U.S. trade with and travel to Cuba for more than six decades. Outlets on the left, center and right covered the confrontation.
stories.background: The United States has kept a trade embargo on Cuba since the early 1960s, after Fidel Castro's revolution, and a 1996 law wrote it into statute. Since 1992 Cuba has asked the U.N. General Assembly every year to call for its end. Last year the resolution passed 165 to 7 with 12 abstentions, with the United States, Israel, Argentina and Hungary among the no votes. Waltz, a former Republican congressman and national security adviser, became U.N. ambassador in 2025.

stories.headline: At least 68 killed as high-speed trains collide near Toledo, Spain's second deadly rail crash this year
stories.summary: A high-speed train ran into another that had stopped on the tracks near Urda, in Spain's Toledo province south of Madrid, on Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens, according to the Castilla-La Mancha regional government. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the site and promised to find out urgently what happened. It is Spain's second deadly rail collision this year, after a January crash in Andalusia killed 46.
stories.why_it_matters: Spain's high-speed trains carry millions of commuters and tourists a year, and a second deadly crash in ten months will put pressure on the government and the rail operators to explain what failed and what they will change.
stories.background: Spain has built Europe's largest high-speed rail network over three decades, and since 2021 private operators have competed with the state rail company, Renfe, on its main routes. In January, a train run by the private operator Iryo derailed near Adamuz in Córdoba province and was struck by a Renfe train; the Financial Times puts that toll at 46. Wednesday's crash happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. Pedro Sánchez leads a Socialist-led government, and Óscar Puente is its transport minister.

In the January crash, near Adamuz in Córdoba province, a train run by the private operator Iryo derailed and was hit by a Renfe train.

stories.headline: Israel's election leaves neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a majority
stories.summary: Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won the 61 seats needed for a majority in Tuesday's Israeli election, partial results show. With more than 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc had 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48 and Arab parties 19, according to The Times of Israel. stories.background: Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset, is elected by nationwide proportional representation, so governments are coalitions that need at least 61 seats. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has led a right-wing and religious coalition since the 2022 election, through the Gaza war that followed Hamas's October 2023 attack and this year's war with Iran. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, heads the main opposition bloc, and his party led Likud in pre-election polls. Arab-led parties have rarely been part of Israeli governments, which is why their seat count matters for any coalition.

stories.headline: Iran rejects ideas in new Qatari peace draft as US reportedly warns Gulf of renewed strikes
stories.summary: Qatari mediators gave Iran a new draft deal on Sunday to end its war with the United States and Israel, an official briefed on the talks said, but an Iranian official said Wednesday that the latest mediation held only unacceptable ideas, Reuters reported. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that the US has warned several Gulf Arab states it may launch a short, intense round of strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: The war has pushed up fuel prices well beyond the Middle East, so whether it ends in a deal or flares up again after the midterms affects what people pay for gasoline, heating and travel. The Pentagon puts the US military's cost so far at more than $47 billion.
stories.background: The United States and Israel have been at war with Iran this year, and US and Israeli strikes have damaged Iranian nuclear sites this year and last. President Trump has said stopping Iran's nuclear program was one of the main reasons for the war. The fighting has raised fuel costs worldwide, and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have been firing missiles at Saudi Arabia.

stories.headline: Fed holds rates steady as two officials vote for a hike
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday at its last meeting before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. stories.why_it_matters: Rates on credit cards, car loans and home-equity lines move with the Fed's benchmark, so borrowing costs stay where they are for now. With inflation rising and two officials already pushing for a hike, the Fed could raise borrowing costs again in December, just as people take on holiday debt.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve sets a short-term interest rate that shapes what banks charge for loans across the economy. It raises the rate to cool inflation and cuts it to support jobs. After cutting rates in 2024 and 2025, the Fed raised them in September for the first time since 2023, as the war with Iran pushed oil and gas prices higher and inflation picked up again. Kevin Warsh, President Trump's pick to succeed Jerome Powell, took over as Fed chair this year. Trump has publicly called for much lower rates and is trying to remove Governor Lisa Cook over mortgage-fraud allegations she denies.

facts.text: The Fed left its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday.

Warsh said politics played "no role" in the decision, which came six days before the midterm elections.
The Fed's statement said officials want to see more information before deciding their next move.
Inflation has sped up in recent months as the Iran war drove up oil and gas prices.
NBC News reported that annual inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August.
Wednesday's hold followed a September increase, the Fed's first rate hike since 2023.
Treasury yields rose ahead of the decision. The 10-year yield was above 5.02% by midmorning, up about 3 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point).
After the September hike, Trump wrote on Truth Social that U.S. interest rates should be 1% or less.
The New York Times reported that Cook, whom Trump is trying to fire, is set to face a private hearing over mortgage-fraud allegations she has consistently denied.

stories.headline: Siena poll puts Hochul 14 points ahead of Blakeman a week before Election Day
stories.summary: A Siena Research Institute poll released Wednesday found Gov. Kathy Hochul leading Republican Bruce Blakeman 54% to 40% among likely voters, up from a 9-point lead in Siena's September survey. The same poll found Mayor Zohran Mamdani's favorability among city voters rising to 69%. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
stories.why_it_matters: The governor shapes the state budget that helps fund city schools and the MTA, and has a say over rent and tax rules the city cannot change alone. The poll also suggests Mamdani, who needs Albany's approval for parts of his agenda such as tax increases, is gaining standing with city voters.
stories.background: Hochul, a Democrat, became governor in 2021 when Andrew Cuomo resigned, and won a full term in 2022 by about 6 points, a narrower margin than some late polls showed. Blakeman, the Republican Nassau County executive, became his party's nominee after Rep. Elise Stefanik left the race. The Siena Research Institute polls New York voters regularly, and its September survey had Hochul ahead 50% to 41%. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, took office as mayor in January.

facts.text: Siena's poll of likely voters, released Wednesday, has Hochul at 54% and Blakeman at 40%, compared with 50% to 41% in Siena's September poll.
Siena surveyed 807 likely voters from Oct. 19 to 22; the margin of error is plus or minus 4.1 percentage points.
Hochul's favorability rating rose to 51% favorable and 45% unfavorable; Siena said it was the first time a majority of likely voters viewed her favorably since she became governor.
Blakeman's rating was 39% favorable and 40% unfavorable, compared with 35% to 34% a month earlier.
Asked who would do more to make New York affordable, 30% chose Hochul, 27% chose Blakeman and 35% said neither.
Hochul led 67% to 23% in New York City, while the race was close in the downstate suburbs (49% to 47%) and upstate (49% to 48%).
Mamdani's favorability among city voters rose to 69% from 60% in September; statewide he stood at 47% favorable and 43% unfavorable.
Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said Blakeman is “running out of time” to close a gap that is growing.

Romero, 62, was arrested and first charged with murder, but prosecutors in District Attorney Alvin Bragg's office reduced the charge to first-degree manslaughter, and Romero pleaded not guilty. The reduction drew objections from Irvine's family and fellow utility workers before the grand jury voted the murder indictment.

stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani moved to replace Linda Tigani as chair of the city's Commission on Racial Equity after she criticized his administration's handling of a racial equity report. City Council members and demonstrators objected, and Gothamist reported that Tigani will stay on through July 2027 under a city rule, though the mayor still plans to put forward Christopher Alexander for the post.
stories.why_it_matters: The commission reviews City Hall's legally required plans to reduce racial disparities in city services, and the dispute is over whether a critic of the mayor keeps overseeing that work. In the brief's feeds only The New York Times covered it; the other coverage found came from left-leaning and center local outlets.
stories.background: City voters approved a ballot measure in 2022 that created the Commission on Racial Equity and required the city to publish racial equity plans on a set schedule. Tigani became chair under Mayor Eric Adams. The commission later sued, arguing that both Adams and Mamdani missed the legal deadline for a plan, and won; the city has appealed. Council Speaker Julie Menin and the Council's Black, Latino and Asian Caucus have backed Tigani.

facts.text: Mamdani sought to replace Tigani as chair of the Commission on Racial Equity; Tigani has criticized the administration's handling of a racial equity report and publicly objected to the plan to remove her.
City Council members spoke out in support of Tigani.
Demonstrators protested the mayor's move to replace her.

Gothamist reported that Tigani will remain chair through July 2027 because city rules extend the chair's term a year if the mayor and Council do not agree on a replacement within 90 days of the term's end.
Speaker Julie Menin sided with the Council's Black, Latino and Asian Caucus in opposing the replacement, Gothamist reported.
Mamdani said he still intends to put forward Christopher Alexander, who leads the NAACP's New York State Conference, as the next chair.
The commission won a lawsuit arguing that Mamdani and Adams missed the legal deadline to release a racial equity plan; the administration has appealed.

stories.headline: Former Brooklyn resident convicted of receiving ISIS military training in Syria
stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday convicted Halima Salman, a 27-year-old U.S. citizen and former Brooklyn resident, of receiving military-type training from ISIS in Syria. She faces up to 10 years in prison and is scheduled to be sentenced Feb. 2. Her lawyers have asked the judge to overturn the verdict.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows how a New York federal court is treating an American who was taken to ISIS territory as a teenager and later came home: jurors weighed evidence of weapons training against the defense's argument that her father and husband drew her in.
stories.background: ISIS held territory across Syria and Iraq from about 2014 until 2019, and thousands of foreigners, including some Americans, went to live under its rule. After its defeat, many women and children linked to the group were held in camps in northeastern Syria, and the U.S. has brought some citizens home and prosecuted some of them. Federal law makes it a crime to knowingly receive military-type training from a designated terrorist group, with a maximum of 10 years in prison. Salman's father took her to ISIS-held territory in 2016, when she was 17, and she returned to the U.S. in 2024.

facts.text: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman on Tuesday of receiving military-type training from ISIS in Syria.
She faces up to 10 years in prison.

Her defense argued she was a teenager drawn into the conflict by her father and later her husband, and her lawyers have asked the judge to set aside the verdict.

markets.summary: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, as expected, but two officials voted for an increase, so a hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting remains possible with inflation at 3.7%, pushed up by oil and gas prices from the Iran war. Stocks closed slightly higher, with the S&P 500 up about 0.3%, while the tech rally set off by Anthropic's filing to go public faded. The 10-year Treasury yield, which guides mortgage rates, held near 5%. After the closing bell, Microsoft shares rose on strong cloud sales, while Alphabet fell about 10% in after-hours trading (trading after the 4 p.m. close) on a profit miss and heavy spending on AI.

concept.explanation: The 10-year Treasury yield is the annual interest the U.S. government pays to borrow money for 10 years. It is set by trading, not by the Fed: when investors expect higher inflation, more government borrowing or higher Fed rates, they demand more interest and the yield rises. It stood at 5.00% on Monday, slightly below where it was a month earlier. Lenders use it as a starting point for long-term loans, which is why the average 30-year mortgage rate (7.32% last week) tends to move with it: when the 10-year yield climbs, buying a home or refinancing gets more expensive, while savers can earn more on bonds and CDs.
